artworks.title: Phèdre (Phaedra)
artworks.description: Shown at the Paris Salon of 1880 and given by the artist to his native Montpellier, this large oil on canvas (194 × 286 cm) is the defining modern image of Phaedra: the Cretan queen, daughter of Minos and wife of Theseus, lies wasted on her bed while two attendants watch her silent agony. Cabanel's academic, faintly Orientalist staging follows Euripides and Racine — the stepmother consumed by forbidden love for Hippolytus — and remains the centrepiece of the Musée Fabre.

artworks.title: Phèdre et Hippolyte (Phaedra and Hippolytus)
artworks.description: Bought by the French state at the Salon of 1802 and now in the Louvre (INV 5182), Guérin's Neoclassical canvas stages Racine's Act IV: Hippolytus denies before Theseus the charge that Phaedra, counselled by Oenone, has laid against him. Marble architecture and hunting dogs frame a palace confrontation in which the stepmother's false accusation seals the curse that will destroy her stepson — a cold, calculated drama that made Guérin's reputation.

artworks.title: Phaedra with an Attendant (Pompeii fresco)
artworks.description: This small Pompeian fresco (21.5 × 28.5 cm) in the British Museum (1856,0625.5) shows Phaedra seated in distress beside a standing attendant, almost certainly her nurse — the go-between of Euripides' tragedy. Recovered from Pompeii and later in the Fejérváry and Bööcke collections, the panel proves how early Roman domestic art already treated the lovesick queen as a recognizable mythic type.

artworks.title: Sarcophagus of Phaedra and Hippolytus
artworks.description: The front of this marble sarcophagus in the Louvre (Ma 2294), found in 1853 on the Chiarone in Tuscany and once in the Campana Collection, narrates the Phaedra cycle in high relief: the queen's passion, the huntress-youth Hippolytus, and the disaster that follows Theseus' curse. Carved about AD 290 at roughly 1.1 × 2.2 m, it shows how late Roman funerary art kept the Euripidean story as a moral and mythic frieze.

artworks.title: Hippolytus, Phaedra and the Nurse
artworks.description: From Herculaneum and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, this First Style–tradition fresco centres the seated, lovesick Phaedra with her aged nurse as go-between, while the chaste Hippolytus stands apart. Buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, the composition preserves a Greek pictorial type that made Phaedra's forbidden passion a favourite subject of Campanian wall decoration.

films.title: Phaedra
films.description: Dassin and Melina Mercouri update the stepmother's desire to a modern Greek shipping dynasty — Phaedra's forbidden love for her husband's son.

films.title: Minotaur, the Wild Beast of Crete
films.description: The peplum keeps Phaedra as Minos' daughter and Ariadne's twin — the Cretan princess whose palace intrigue frames Theseus' arrival and the labyrinth.

music.title: Hippolyte et Aricie
music.description: Rameau's first opera stages Phaedra's passion and Theseus' curse — the stepmother's confession that destroys Hippolytus.

music.title: Fedra
music.description: Pizzetti sets D'Annunzio's Phaedra at La Scala — the queen's unrequited love for Hippolytus sung as Italian verismo tragedy.

music.title: Phaedra
music.description: Britten's last vocal work is a cantata of Racine's confessions — Phaedra's guilt and desire scored for mezzo-soprano, harpsichord and small orchestra.

popCulture.title: Phèdre
popCulture.creator: Jean Racine
popCulture.description: Racine's tragedy is the French Phaedra: guilt, desire and the confession that kills, still the standard modern stage face of the myth.

popCulture.title: Phaedra
popCulture.creator: Seneca
popCulture.description: Seneca's Roman tragedy hardens Phaedra's passion into Stoic catastrophe — the stepmother whose accusation and suicide frame Hippolytus' death.

popCulture.title: Phaedra's Love
popCulture.creator: Sarah Kane
popCulture.description: Kane's brutal Gate Theatre rewrite after Seneca keeps Phaedra's desire as modern nihilism — love as violence, the court as a slaughterhouse.

popCulture.title: Desire Under the Elms
popCulture.creator: Eugene O'Neill
popCulture.description: O'Neill transplants Phaedra's passion to a New England farm — the stepmother's desire for her husband's son rewritten as American tragedy.

popCulture.title: The Bull from the Sea
popCulture.creator: Mary Renault
popCulture.description: Renault's sequel gives Phaedra the Cretan marriage that undoes Theseus — the stepmother whose desire for Hippolytus closes the king's story.
